html:
The Farmer's Law is a short Byzantine legal text of rules for village life, probably written in the late 7th or the 8th century. Its date and author are unknown. It deals with the everyday troubles of farmers: stolen or injured animals, damage to crops and vineyards, swaps of fields, and quarrels between neighbours.

It is valuable because it shows a world of free peasants in villages that paid their taxes together, at a time when the Byzantine Empire was fighting for survival against the Arab conquests and Slavic settlement in the Balkans. Punishments include fines, whipping and for some crimes mutilation, much as in the Ecloga, and some scholars link the two.

Older historians read it as proof that Slavic settlers had brought new village customs into the empire. Most now see it as a summary of local custom resting on Roman law. It was often copied alongside later law books, such as the Hexabiblos.
